title: Interrupts and polling
text: When a packet lands, something has to notice. Either the card interrupts a core, or a core is already watching. That choice is worth microseconds.

title: The interrupt path
text: The card writes the packet into memory and raises an interrupt. The core drops what it was doing, and the kernel's NAPI code processes the packet, then wakes the thread waiting on the socket. AMD's Onload guide says answering an interrupt and switching to the right thread can take on the order of a microsecond. A core already spinning on the queue can start in nanoseconds. Each step is quick on its own, but they add up, and they add jitter.

title: Interrupt coalescing
text: To save CPU, cards coalesce interrupts. With ethtool -C, rx-usecs sets how long to wait after a packet arrives, and rx-frames how many packets to collect, before interrupting. Adaptive mode tunes both on the fly. That is great for throughput, but the first packet of a burst now waits for the timer. For a trading feed, that timer is pure added latency.

title: Busy polling
text: Busy polling turns this around. With the SO_BUSY_POLL socket option, or the busy_poll sysctls, a thread checks the device queue itself before the interrupt fires. Kernel bypass stacks go further, and spin entirely in user space: Onload's EF_POLL_USEC spins for up to that many microseconds before it blocks. The cost is a core at 100 percent, all day long. On a shared or virtual machine, a spinning thread also takes time from its neighbours.

title: IRQ affinity
text: Where interrupts land matters too. With receive side scaling, the card hashes each flow onto a queue, and each queue has its own interrupt. You can pin that interrupt to a chosen core through /proc/irq. Keep it away from your trading cores, and remember that irqbalance can move it back. Check where each one lands, and check again after a reboot.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's core plan gives every hot thread a core of its own. The feed's receive thread is on CPU 2, the book on 3, trading on 4, and order entry on 5. Each one spins. The receive thread calls a non-blocking recvmmsg in a loop, and sleeps only if its config sets an idle sleep, which is meant for processes off the hot path. On the lab's shared box, two busy-polling processes passed a 64 byte message over Aeron and back in 0.72 to 0.81 microseconds at the median.

title: Takeaway
text: Interrupts trade latency for CPU time. On the hot path, buy the latency back: spin on a dedicated core, and send the interrupts somewhere else. Next: how to see what really happened on the wire.
